extracted.intended_audience: research mathematicians and graduate students in combinatorics, convexity, and metric/geometric combinatorics
extracted.subtask_description: A list of open problems and questions around Borsuk’s conjecture (behavior of the covering function f(d), low-dimensional cases, metric/elliptic embeddings, and related combinatorial conjectures) aimed at researchers and students. Each numbered item poses a precise question or line of investigation and includes brief context and pointers to known results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asymptotic behavior of f(d)
rubrics_metrics.description: What is the asymptotic behavior of f(d)?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Improving the lower bound: The best lower bound are of the form . The best known value of C was found by Andrei Raigorodskii. In the previous post I presented a speculative approach towards improving the exponent from to a higher power of . Is the true exponent one? Improving the upper bound: The best asymptotic upper bound is of the form . There are two different proofs for this result. The first by Oded Schramm is based on covering a set of constant width by smaller homothets. The second by Jean Bourgain and Joram Lindenstrauss is based by covering a set of diameter 1 by balls of diameter 1. There is a result by Danzer showing that we need at least balls of diameter 1 to cover an arbitrary set of diameter 1 in .

rubrics_metrics.name: Low-dimensional cases (dimension 4 and other small d)
rubrics_metrics.description: Is there a counterexample in dimension 4? What is the smallest (stated as 'lated') d for which Borsuk’s conjecture is false?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This asks for explicit constructions or impossibility results in small fixed dimensions, and determination of the minimal dimension where Borsuk's conjecture fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order-preserving embeddings for the elliptic metric space
rubrics_metrics.description: Study embeddings of the elliptic n-dimensional space (lines through the origin in R^n with distance the smaller angle between them) into Euclidean R^d that preserve the order relation between distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: Frankl–Wilson’s theorem implies an exponential lower bound in n for . The crux for the counterexample is an embedding from the elliptic space to Euclidean space that preserves the order relation between distances: so that if one pair of lines is farther than another in the elliptic metric then the images have the same order. The embedding is described (in the post) by a simple map given by . (As a matter of fact we need this property to hold just for the case that and are of maximum distance.) Problem: Let be an order preserving embedding of the elliptic n-dimensional space into a d-dimensional Euclidean space. Does it follow that d is at least quadratic in n? The post notes metric embeddings are heavily studied but order-preserving (ranking) embeddings have been less explored.

rubrics_metrics.name: Larman's conjecture
rubrics_metrics.description: Larman’s conjecture: Let F be a family of k-subsets of [n]. Suppose that every two sets in F have at least t elements in common; then F can be divided into at most n families so that every two sets in each of these families have at least t elements in common.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remarks: Larman observed that Borsuk’s conjecture implies Larman’s conjecture. The post notes that while Borsuk’s conjecture once seemed correct, Larman’s conjecture did not, and asks: Is Larman’s conjecture for t=1 correct? (i.e., the specific case of pairwise intersection at least 1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Erdős–Faber–Lovász (EFL) related question
rubrics_metrics.description: A question closely resembling the t=1 case of Larman’s conjecture is the Erdős–Faber–Lovász Conjecture: Let F be a family of k-subsets of [n]. Suppose that every two sets in F have at most one element in common, then F can be divided into at most n families so that every two sets in each of these families are disjoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The post presents EFL as a closely related combinatorial partitioning conjecture and places it in the same family of questions about partitioning set-systems under intersection constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Borsuk's conjecture for two-distance sets
rubrics_metrics.description: Prove (or disprove) the assertion of Borsuk’s conjecture for two-distance sets: sets in R^d that realize only two distances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Problem originally posed by David Larman in the 1970s. The post asks to establish whether Borsuk’s statement holds when restricted to two-distance sets. (A later comment on the post notes that Borsuk’s conjecture for two-distance sets is also false and references a construction coming from a strongly regular graph G2(4).)
